file.note: The inventory is `pytest --collect-only -q` on the source at 65f36c5, in collection order; all 11 pass there (measured 2026-08-28 against the shared read-only clone of interlock at 65f36c5, `PYTHONPATH=src PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python3 -m pytest -q tests/canary/ -p no:cacheprovider`: 70 passed, of which 11 are tests/canary/test_routing.py's).

systematic_mappings.why: better-sqlite3 raises one SqliteError type for everything, so the Python exception CLASS has no counterpart; the result code is what carries the distinction the class carried (D-0016). The regex is the whole SQLITE_CONSTRAINT family because that is exactly the width of sqlite3.IntegrityError — narrowing it to the constraint that actually fires would assert more than the source does (rule 0). Matches the precedent already set in test/canary/ledger.test.ts.
systematic_mappings.affects: the two ported cases 'a non ownership integrity failure passes through as itself' and 'an idempotent retry does not absorb a validation failure'

systematic_mappings.from: `if "UNIQUE constraint failed: run_owner.run_id" not in str(error): raise`
systematic_mappings.to: `sqliteCodeOf(error)` in {SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_PRIMARYKEY, SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE}, then confirmed by re-reading run_owner
systematic_mappings.why: D-0402 / D-0016 ban message-substring classification: SQLite's message text is not a compatibility surface and its codes are. Measured here, the two do not even agree — the code is PRIMARYKEY, the message says UNIQUE. Not a weakening: the code test is followed by the same re-read the source does, so the classification is confirmed against the store rather than against a string.
systematic_mappings.affects: src/canary/routing.ts `isAlreadyRoutedConflict`; the behaviour of every route_run_start conflict path

systematic_mappings.to: an exported `interface` plus `Object.freeze({...})` assembled by COLUMN NAME from a typed row shape
systematic_mappings.why: TypeScript has no frozen dataclass; a readonly interface plus a frozen literal gives the same observable (structural equality under toEqual, no mutation). Reading by name rather than by position is the same mapping written down, and it cannot silently swap two same-typed fields if a SELECT list is ever reordered — the hazard the brief names. The SELECT column lists are kept in the source's order regardless.

systematic_mappings.from: `with self._connection:` (a commit/rollback scope over sqlite3's implicit deferred transaction)
systematic_mappings.why: better-sqlite3 has no implicit transaction — a bare `.run()` autocommits — so 'every method is one transaction' would be lost without an explicit wrapper, and the `changes === 0` refusal would fire after the insert had already committed. Applied to routeNewRunsTo and routeRunStart only; currentDecision and routedRun stay untransacted, as in the source.

systematic_mappings.from: `f"{owning_system!r}"` and `f"...{OWNING_SYSTEMS}"` (Python repr of a str, and of a 2-tuple)
systematic_mappings.to: a private string-only `repr()` and a single precomputed `OWNING_SYSTEMS_REPR` constant
systematic_mappings.why: D-0017 rule 3 (Python repr becomes hand-written quotes, never JSON.stringify — which would give ["interlock","synthetic_v1"] and the wrong quote character) and rule 4 (one renderer for an interpolated tuple, not an inline join per call site). The repo's shared pythonRepr was deliberately NOT imported; see concerns for why and for the trade.
systematic_mappings.affects: the UnknownOwningSystem, OwnerChangeRefused and UnroutedRun messages

systematic_mappings.to: a plain `routingFixture()` call returning both, with `onTestFinished` registering a close that tolerates an already-closed handle
systematic_mappings.why: House pattern, copied from test/canary/ledger.test.ts. Function scope, per test, which is what pytest's function-scoped fixtures give; the tolerant close matches Python's close-a-closed-connection no-op.

The case's whole subject is a value the declared parameter type excludes, so it has to be pushed past the type in both languages. `as unknown as number` is TypeScript's `# type: ignore[arg-type]`; there is no weaker cast that reaches the store.
systematic_mappings.affects: 'an idempotent retry does not absorb a validation failure'

target_only_tests.why: target-only -- the duplicate run conflict is the replacement guard, not the primary key (renamed and re-pointed by D-0406; it pinned D-0402's factual basis before the D-0405 guard landed). The two ported cases that would notice an OVER-broad classification only ever exercise CHECK, so nothing in the source's suite can notice a TOO-NARROW one, and nothing anywhere records WHY the accepted set has two members. This case issues route_run_start's own statement directly. It asserted the D-0402 disagreement -- code SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_PRIMARYKEY under a message reading 'UNIQUE constraint failed: run_owner.run_id' -- and since the D-0405 guard fires ahead of conflict resolution it now asserts what a duplicate actually meets: SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_TRIGGER, the guard's sentence, and no UNIQUE message at all. A future reader who removes the guard, or who reads D-0402 without D-0406, gets a red test naming the change rather than a routing point that silently stopped recognising its own retries. target-only -- a retry under a later decision naming the same owner returns the original row: The source's docstring states that decision_seq is deliberately NOT compared, but its idempotency case never flips the policy in between, so its suite cannot distinguish 'compares owningSystem' from 'compares the whole row'. Measured: adding an `existing.decisionSeq === decision.decisionSeq` conjunct leaves all 11 ported cases green and turns only this one red. It asserts the original decisionSeq (1) and routedAtMs (T0+1) survive a retry under decision 2. target-only -- an unknown owning system is refused before anything is written: The source's vocabulary case asserts only that UnknownOwningSystem is raised. 'Nothing was written' is RoutingRefused's documented base-class contract and the reason the membership test precedes the transaction, and the store's own CHECK would refuse a third system too — so without this case the API-layer refusal and the store-layer refusal are indistinguishable. It goes beside the faithful case rather than being folded into it (rule 0). Measured: disabling the membership check turns both this case and the ported one red, with 'got SqliteError: CHECK constraint failed: owning_system IN (...)'. target-only -- a decision sequence past 2**53 survives the round trip: D-0407. `routeNewRunsTo` narrowed `lastInsertRowid` with `Number(...)` and both reads returned plain doubles, so a `decision_seq` the schema permits but a double cannot hold came back off by one, presented as the store's own value. Python's `int` is arbitrary precision, so this was the port's defect and not interlock's, and no source case can reach it: the writer that can is the out-of-package one D-0405 is about, which is what `rawConnection` is here. Measured: with `safeIntegers` removed the case reads 9007199254740992 and goes red naming the loss. Every value inside the safe range is narrowed back to `number`, which the ported cases assert with `toBe(1)` and `toBe(3)` -- assertions a bigint fails -- so the widening is visible only where the alternative was a wrong answer.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: `routeRunStart`'s post-conflict re-reads can themselves throw. If another connection deletes the run_owner row (or the whole routing policy) between the UNIQUE/PRIMARYKEY failure and the re-read, the caller sees `UnroutedRun` or `NoRoutingDecision` rather than a conflict-specific refusal.
inherited_limitations.why: The source has exactly this shape (`existing = self.routed_run(run_id)` / `decision = self.current_decision()` both raise), and both are RoutingRefused subclasses so the base-class contract still holds. Reproduced rather than repaired: a repair here would be new code with no warrant (rule 11), and the store's delete triggers make the state unreachable through the module's own API anyway.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: `nowMs` is typed `number`, which admits NaN, Infinity and fractional values that Python's `int` excluded (rule 9). No guard was added.
inherited_limitations.why: The store already refuses every one of them and refuses them as itself: a fractional or Infinity value binds as REAL and trips `CHECK (typeof(...) = 'integer')`; NaN binds as NULL and trips NOT NULL. So the wider type produces a refusal, never a silently-accepted bad row, and adding an API-layer guard would introduce a refusal type the source does not have and change which error the ninth ported case sees. Recorded here rather than fixed; flagging it for the integrator as the answer to rule 9's second question.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: `isAlreadyRoutedConflict` accepts a uniqueness code from the statement without checking WHICH constraint produced it.
inherited_limitations.why: The source has the same reach through its substring, only narrower by accident of message text. It is sound on this DDL — `ROUTE_RUN_START_SQL` writes only `run_owner`, whose only uniqueness is `run_id` — and the code is not trusted alone: the caller confirms by re-reading the row, and an absent row surfaces as UnroutedRun rather than as a fabricated conflict. Since D-0406 the accepted set also holds SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_TRIGGER, which is NOT specific to one constraint -- five triggers in the DDL raise it -- so that code alone is not allowed to stand: the row is re-read first, and an absent row means another trigger fired and the error passes through as itself. The two uniqueness codes keep the shape described above unchanged.

divergences.behaviour: `isAlreadyRoutedConflict` accepts SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_TRIGGER in addition to _PRIMARYKEY and _UNIQUE, and `routeRunStart` re-reads the run_owner row before reading a _TRIGGER failure as an ownership question. interlock classifies the same conflict by substring-matching 'UNIQUE constraint failed: run_owner.run_id'.
divergences.note: Forced by D-0405's repair, not chosen: `run_owner_is_never_replaced` is a BEFORE INSERT trigger and BEFORE INSERT triggers fire ahead of conflict resolution, which is exactly what closes the INSERT OR REPLACE hole and exactly what puts the trigger ahead of the primary key. D-0402's decision is otherwise unchanged. The confirmation step exists because _TRIGGER, unlike the two uniqueness codes, is raised by five triggers in this DDL including one on this very statement, so it proposes rather than decides.
divergences.parity_cost: None on any path a source case exercises: all 11 ported cases are green and unchanged, including the two that pin the classification's width from the other side ('a non ownership integrity failure passes through as itself' and 'an idempotent retry does not absorb a validation failure'). The observable behaviour of route_run_start -- idempotent retry, OwnerChangeRefused, everything else rethrown as itself -- is the same; only which result code arrives has moved.
divergences.evidence: test/canary/routing.test.ts::classification by result code, not message text (target-only) > target-only -- the duplicate run conflict is the replacement guard, not the primary key; and test/canary/ledger.test.ts::store enforcement on every connection (target-only) > target-only -- the replacement guard defers to the row's own CHECKs, which pins the property that keeps the validation case landing.

divergences.behaviour: The routing point's three statements run with `safeIntegers(true)` and narrow each integer back to `number` only when a double holds it exactly; `RoutingDecision.decisionSeq` / `.decidedAtMs` and `RoutedRun.decisionSeq` / `.routedAtMs` are `number | bigint`. interlock's dataclasses hold Python `int`s and lose nothing, so there is nothing here to translate.
divergences.note: Port-introduced, raised as [P2] by the review gate on the canary belt's final round and recorded there as knowingly left, with a pointer to this change. Repaired here rather than left because D-0023 does not distinguish a defect by who introduced it, and because this is the change where the classification it sits beside was being re-decided anyway. The same five-line rule `src/canary/audit.ts` applies to the digest and the rollback rows; it is duplicated rather than imported for the reason routing.ts's `repr` is duplicated -- this module's import poverty is a documented, structurally asserted property.
divergences.parity_cost: None observable for any ledger this package can write: every sequence and timestamp a continuo API produces is inside the safe range and comes back a `number`, exactly as before. A ledger written out of band with a value past 2**53 now reads back correctly instead of off by one.
